tldr:
**Commands and skills are / workflows you invoke.**

- **Team ones** go in the repository: `.claude/commands/` or `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`.
- **Personal ones** go in `~/.claude/skills/`, under a **different name** from the team's.

**Frontmatter:**

- **`context: fork`** runs a verbose skill in an isolated subagent, so only the result comes back.
- **`argument-hint`** tells developers which parameter to pass.
- **Tool limits:** the guide says `allowed-tools`. ⚠️ In current Claude Code, `allowed-tools` **pre-approves** tools and **`disallowed-tools` removes them**.

**Skill vs CLAUDE.md:** use a **skill** for on-demand tasks and **CLAUDE.md** for standards every task needs.
mentalModel: A skill is a recipe card in the shared kitchen drawer (.claude/skills/) — everyone can pull it out when they cook that dish. Your own twist goes on a card in your apron pocket with a different name, not scribbled over the shared card. CLAUDE.md is the sign on the wall everybody sees every time. context: fork cooks in the back kitchen and sends out only the plate.
whatItIs:
The exam guide covers creating and configuring custom slash commands and skills (Guide §6 · TS 3.2, p.13). The skills docs
define every frontmatter field — in one place differently from the guide (see the ⚠️ table).

**Sub-concepts — each with its picture to remember**

| # | Sub-concept | 🧭 Mental model | ⭐ Exam reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Project commands `.claude/commands/` | A recipe card in the shared drawer — everyone has it. | ⭐ TS 3.2 · Knowledge 1, Skill 1 |
| 2 | User commands `~/.claude/commands/` | A card in your apron pocket — only you have it. | ⭐ TS 3.2 · Knowledge 1 |
| 3 | Skills `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` | A recipe card with notes in the margin (frontmatter). | ⭐ TS 3.2 · Knowledge 2 |
| 4 | `context: fork` | Cook in the back kitchen; send out only the plate. | ⭐ TS 3.2 · Knowledge 3, Skill 2 |
| 5 | Limiting tools | Lock the knife drawer while this recipe runs. | ⭐ TS 3.2 · Skill 3 (see ⚠️ below) |
| 6 | `argument-hint` | “Serves: __” printed on the card, so nobody forgets to fill it in. | ⭐ TS 3.2 · Skill 4 |
| 7 | Personal variant, new name | Your twist on your own card, not scribbled on the shared one. | ⭐ TS 3.2 · Knowledge 4 |
| 8 | Skill vs CLAUDE.md | A recipe you pull out when needed vs the sign on the wall everyone sees. | ⭐ TS 3.2 · Skill 5 |
| 9 | `disable-model-invocation` | A card only a person may pull out (deploy, commit). | 📘 docs |

**⚠️ Tool limits — the guide's wording vs current Claude Code**

| # | Question | Exam guide (TS 3.2 Skill 3) | Claude Code docs (2026-09-28) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which field restricts tools during a skill? | `allowed-tools` | **`disallowed-tools`** removes tools while the skill is active |
| 2 | What does `allowed-tools` do? | Restricts tool access | **Pre-approves** the listed tools for that turn — “does not restrict which tools are available” |
| 3 | How long does it last? | — | Until you send your next message |
| 4 | For an exam answer | ⭐ Pick **allowed-tools** for “restrict tools in a skill” | — |
| 5 | In a real skill | — | `allowed-tools` to skip prompts **+** `disallowed-tools` to take tools away |

**Where commands and skills live**

| # | Location | Who gets it | In git? | Same name wins? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `.claude/commands/<name>.md` | The team | Yes | A skill with the same name wins over it |
| 2 | `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` | The team | Yes | Personal beats project |
| 3 | `~/.claude/commands/`, `~/.claude/skills/` | Only you, all projects | No | Personal beats project (docs) — so use a **new name** for variants |
| 4 | Enterprise (managed) | Everyone in the organisation | — | Beats personal |

**Frontmatter fields the exam names** (plus two docs-only fields)

| # | Field | Does (docs) | Use it for |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ⭐ `context: fork` (+ `agent`) | Runs in an isolated subagent, no conversation history; the result returns | Verbose analysis, brainstorming |
| 2 | ⭐ `allowed-tools` | Pre-approves tools for the turn | Skipping prompts (guide: restricting) |
| 3 | `disallowed-tools` | Removes tools while the skill is active | Actually taking tools away |
| 4 | ⭐ `argument-hint` | Shown in autocomplete, e.g. `[issue-number]` | Required parameters |
| 5 | `disable-model-invocation` | Only a person can invoke it | Deploy, commit, side effects |
howItWorks:
1. **Always needed?** Put it in CLAUDE.md. **A task someone invokes?** Make it a command or skill.
2. **For the team?** Put it in `.claude/commands/` or `.claude/skills/` in git. **Just you?** Use `~/.claude/skills/`, with
   a new name if it's a variant of a team skill.
3. **Verbose or exploratory?** Add `context: fork` (and `agent: Explore` for read-only work).
4. **Risky tools?** Take them away with `disallowed-tools`; pre-approve safe ones with `allowed-tools`. The guide calls this
   "allowed-tools".
5. **Needs a parameter?** Add an `argument-hint` and use `$ARGUMENTS` in the body.

grounding.text: Skill locations: enterprise (managed), personal ~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md (all your projects), project .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md (this repository), nested, plugin (/plugin:name), bundled. Same name: enterprise over personal, personal over project; a skill over a .claude/commands/ file.
Custom commands in .claude/commands/ still work; skills add supporting files, frontmatter control and automatic invocation. Both create / commands.
context: fork runs the skill in an isolated subagent with no conversation history; `agent` picks the subagent type (e.g. Explore); the result returns to the main conversation.

allowed-tools lists tools Claude can use without asking during the turn that invokes the skill; the grant clears on your next message; it does not restrict which tools are available — every tool stays callable.
grounding.ref: skills § Pre-approve tools for a skill

grounding.text: disallowed-tools removes tools from Claude's available pool while the skill is active; the restriction clears on your next message.

argument-hint is shown during autocomplete to indicate expected arguments (e.g. [issue-number]); $ARGUMENTS expands to what was typed; if no placeholder receives an argument, Claude Code appends ARGUMENTS: <value>.
disable-model-invocation: true — only you can invoke the skill (for /deploy, /commit and other side effects).
CLAUDE.md loads every session; a skill's description loads each session and its full content when used.

grounding.text: In acceptEdits mode, file edits and filesystem commands (mkdir, touch, rm, rmdir, mv, cp, sed) inside the working directory are auto-approved.

Project commands in .claude/commands/ are shared via version control; user commands in ~/.claude/commands/ are personal; skills in .claude/skills/ with SKILL.md support frontmatter (context: fork, allowed-tools, argument-hint); context: fork isolates skill output from the main conversation; personal variants go in ~/.claude/skills/ with different names.

Skills: project commands for team availability; context: fork for verbose or exploratory skills; allowed-tools to restrict tool access during a skill; argument-hint to prompt for required parameters; skills for on-demand workflows vs CLAUDE.md for always-loaded standards.

The guide says allowed-tools restricts tool access; the docs say allowed-tools pre-approves and disallowed-tools restricts. For exam answers use the guide's wording; in real skills use disallowed-tools to take tools away.
Token counts, the scaffold skill's stray rm -rf, the developer following the argument hint and the unmatched request are invented.

examPoints.text: Project commands in .claude/commands/ are shared via version control; user commands in ~/.claude/commands/ are personal.
Skills live in .claude/skills/ with a SKILL.md whose frontmatter supports context: fork, allowed-tools and argument-hint.
context: fork runs a skill in an isolated sub-agent so its output doesn't pollute the main conversation.
Personal variants go in ~/.claude/skills/ under different names so teammates aren't affected.
Create project-scoped commands in .claude/commands/ for team-wide availability.
Use context: fork for skills with verbose output (codebase analysis) or exploratory context (brainstorming).
Configure allowed-tools in skill frontmatter to restrict tool access during the skill (e.g. only file writes).

variants.label: ✅ ⭐ team commands in git · fork verbose skills · take risky tools away · argument-hint · CLAUDE.md for standards
variants.code:
from utils.skills_lab import TEAM_REVIEW, simulate   # SIMULATED command/skill loader + sessions

PROJECT = {   # in the repository - every teammate gets these
    # a team command, shared through git
    ".claude/commands/review-pr.md": TEAM_REVIEW,
    # verbose output -> run it in an isolated subagent; only the summary comes back
    ".claude/skills/analyze-codebase/SKILL.md": ("---\nname: analyze-codebase\n"
        "description: Maps every module and dependency in the codebase\ncontext: fork\nagent: Explore\n---\n"
        "Map every module and its dependencies. Return a one-page summary."),
    # only file writing: pre-approve Write/Edit, and REMOVE Bash while the skill runs
    ".claude/skills/scaffold/SKILL.md": ("---\nname: scaffold\ndescription: Creates boilerplate files for a new component\n"
        "allowed-tools: Write Edit\ndisallowed-tools: Bash\n---\nCreate the component, its test and its story."),
    # needs an issue number -> show it in autocomplete, use it via $ARGUMENTS
    ".claude/skills/fix-issue/SKILL.md": ("---\nname: fix-issue\ndescription: Fixes a GitHub issue by number\n"
        "argument-hint: [issue-number]\ndisable-model-invocation: true\n---\nFix issue $ARGUMENTS: reproduce it, fix it, add a test."),
}
CLAUDE_MD = "# Project\n- Use pnpm, never npm.\n"   # a universal standard: always loaded

USER = {   # ~/.claude/ on your machine - a personal variant with its OWN name
    "~/.claude/skills/review-pr-terse/SKILL.md": ("---\nname: review-pr-terse\ndescription: My terse PR review\n---\n"
        "Review the PR; report only blocking issues, one line each."),
}

simulate(PROJECT, USER, CLAUDE_MD)
variants.observe: team_command: a fresh clone has /review-pr. verbose_analysis: /analyze-codebase runs in a forked Explore subagent → +2,000 tokens. restrict_tools: Bash isn't available while /scaffold runs → build/ survives. missing_argument: autocomplete shows [issue-number] → “Fix issue 4521 …”. always_standard: “run the tests” → pnpm test. personal_variant: the team's /review-pr is unchanged; you also have /review-pr-terse.
variants.why: Each piece is where its audience can see it, and does only what its frontmatter allows.

questions.q: A team lead created a /release-notes command in ~/.claude/commands/ and told the 12-person team to use it. Two days later, eleven teammates say the command doesn't exist in their sessions. What is the fix?
opts: Ask each teammate to copy the file from a shared drive into their own ~/.claude/commands/ directory.
Move it to the project's .claude/commands/ and commit it, so everyone gets it through version control.
Paste the command's instructions into CLAUDE.md, so that every teammate's session loads them at start-up.
Have every teammate restart Claude Code, since new commands appear only after a restart.
questions.explain: ~/.claude/commands/ is personal. The project's .claude/commands/ is version-controlled and reaches everyone who clones or pulls. A works but drifts, because every copy is maintained by hand. C turns an on-demand workflow into always-loaded context. D: the file was never on their machines, so a restart changes nothing.

questions.q: A /map-dependencies skill prints about 4,000 lines of analysis into the conversation, crowding out the developer's actual task. The developer only needs the final summary. A teammate proposes adding “be concise” to the skill's instructions. What is the best change?
opts: Add “be concise” as proposed, and cap the skill's output with a maximum line count in its own instructions.
Run /compact after each use of the skill, so that the 4,000 lines are summarised before work continues.
Add context: fork to the skill's frontmatter, so it runs in an isolated sub-agent and returns its result.
Split the skill into four smaller skills, each of which prints one quarter of the dependency analysis.
questions.explain: context: fork runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent. The verbose work stays there, and only the result returns to the main conversation. A may cut the analysis the summary depends on. B pays for the output first and then summarises it lossily. D produces the same 4,000 lines in four pieces.

questions.q: A /generate-docs skill should only write documentation files, but in 3 of its last 20 runs it also ran shell commands that reformatted source code. The team wants to limit which tools the skill uses while it runs. Which frontmatter field does the exam guide use for this?
opts: context: fork, so that the skill runs in a sub-agent that cannot reach the main session's tools.
argument-hint, so the developer states which files the skill may write each time they invoke it.
model, set to a smaller model that is less likely to decide on its own to run shell commands.
allowed-tools, listing only the tools the skill needs, such as Read and Write.
questions.explain: The guide uses allowed-tools in skill frontmatter to restrict tool access during the skill. Current docs add a detail: allowed-tools pre-approves the tools it lists, and disallowed-tools is what removes a tool entirely (see the docs item below). A isolates context, not tools. B only documents the arguments. D hopes a smaller model behaves better.

questions.q: Developers keep invoking /fix-issue without the issue number. In 30% of runs Claude fixes whichever open issue it guesses was meant, and twice it fixed the wrong one before anyone noticed. Which frontmatter addition helps most?
opts: argument-hint: [issue-number]
context: fork
allowed-tools: Read, Edit
description: Fixes GitHub issues
questions.explain: argument-hint shows developers the expected parameter when they invoke the command, so the issue number gets supplied. B isolates the context, C limits tools, and D describes the skill. None of them prompts for the missing argument.

questions.q: A developer wants a terser version of the team's shared /review-pr skill for their own use. The shared skill is used by 15 teammates, who are happy with it as it is. What should the developer do?
opts: Create a personal variant under a different name in ~/.claude/skills/.
Edit the shared skill in .claude/skills/, adding a flag that switches on the terser output.
Ask Claude to be terser each time they run /review-pr, and leave both skill files as they are.
Copy the skill into ~/.claude/skills/ under the same name, so their copy stands in for the team's.
questions.explain: A personal skill in ~/.claude/skills/ with its own name gives the developer their variant and leaves the team's skill untouched. B changes a shared file for one person. C repeats the same instruction every time. D reuses the name, which makes it unclear which version runs. The guide's pattern is a differently named variant.

questions.q: A skill's frontmatter lists allowed-tools: Read, Write, yet during the skill Claude still runs a Bash command after asking the developer's permission. The developer expected Bash to be impossible and files a bug report. Under the current docs, what explains this, and what would block Bash?
opts: It's a bug: allowed-tools should hide every other tool, so reinstalling Claude Code restores the behaviour.
Bash is always available to skills for safety reasons, and no skill frontmatter field can block it.
allowed-tools pre-approves listed tools but doesn't remove others; disallowed-tools would remove Bash.
The skill must also set context: fork, because tool limits apply only to skills that run in a sub-agent.
questions.explain: In current docs, allowed-tools pre-approves the listed tools, and other tools still ask for permission. disallowed-tools removes a tool. The guide simplifies this as “restrict”. A, B and D describe behaviour the docs don't.

faq.q: Commands or skills — which should I create?
faq.a: Both create / commands, and .claude/commands/ files still work. Skills add a folder for supporting files, frontmatter, and automatic invocation when a request matches their description. If both share a name, the skill wins.

faq.q: So which answer do I give on the exam for “restrict tools in a skill”?
faq.a: allowed-tools — that's the guide's wording (TS 3.2 Skill 3). In current Claude Code, allowed-tools pre-approves tools. disallowed-tools is what removes them. This workbench teaches both and logs the difference in docs/SOURCES.md.

faq.q: What does context: fork NOT carry over?
faq.a: The conversation history. The forked subagent sees only the skill's content as its task, so write self-contained instructions. Choose the subagent with `agent` (Explore for read-only analysis).

faq.q: Why a different name for a personal variant?
faq.a: The guide says so, to avoid affecting teammates. The docs add that a personal skill with the same name overrides the project one for you, so you'd silently stop getting the team's version.
